case.background: Monochromatic light illuminates a clean cathode in a vacuum phototube. Vary frequency and the absorbed photon rate, then use stopping potential and saturation current to explain when and how electrons are emitted.
initial_observations: Some illumination settings produce no measurable photocurrent.
When electrons are emitted, a reverse voltage can stop the current.

controls.description: Absorbed photon rate at the cathode relative to the reference setting.
controls.name: absorbed_photon_flux_relative

instruments.description: A clean-cathode vacuum phototube with monochromatic illumination and electrical meters.
instruments.name: vacuum_phototube

notes: The cathode remains clean and unchanged across experiments.
When a work function is reported in volts, it denotes the energy divided by elementary charge.
The photon-flux control is absorbed photon rate, not optical power or irradiance.
Above threshold, the ideal cathode has frequency-independent quantum yield and the saturation circuit collects every emitted electron.
Zero current and stopping potential mean no emitted electrons.

FinalSubmission.model must equal 'expression'. FinalSubmission.parameters must equal {'outputs': {READOUT: EXPR, ...}} with exactly these readouts: stopping_potential_v, saturation_current_ua. EXPR is the shared family-neutral JSON arithmetic tree over public controls. Supported operators are: add, subtract, multiply, divide, power, negate, exp, log, sin, maximum, step. No candidate law family or truth-specific parameter slots are supplied.

readouts.description: Reverse-potential magnitude needed to reduce photocurrent to zero.
readouts.name: stopping_potential_v

readouts.description: Saturation photocurrent with all emitted electrons collected.
readouts.name: saturation_current_ua

experiment.apparatus: Clean-cathode vacuum phototube with monochromatic illumination. Sequentially measure each of the six settings: (frequency_thz, absorbed_photon_flux_relative) = (500,0.5), (500,2.0), (700,0.5), (700,2.0), (800,0.5), (800,2.0). For each setting sweep reverse voltage to zero current, then measure saturation current with all emitted electrons collected.
experiment.intent: Measure stopping potential and saturation current over frequencies on both sides of the proposed thresholds and at two absorbed photon fluxes, testing frequency-dependent electron energy and flux-dependent emission magnitude.

hypotheses.statement: Each photon ejects an electron only when frequency exceeds a threshold set by a 2.00 eV work function; above threshold stopping potential is 0.0041357 times frequency in THz minus 2.00 V, independent of absorbed photon flux, and saturation current is 1.00 microampere times relative absorbed photon flux.

Emission begins only above a 600 THz threshold; above threshold stopping potential is 0.50 V times relative absorbed photon flux, while saturation current is 1.00 microampere times relative absorbed photon flux.

final.explanation: The observations and supplied candidate laws support a photon-energy threshold: frequency controls electron maximum energy and stopping potential, while absorbed photon flux controls emission rate and saturation current. The requested phototube instrument was unavailable, so no additional evidence could be obtained.
scope_conditions: The cathode is clean and remains unchanged.
The illumination is monochromatic and absorbed by the cathode in vacuum.
The saturation circuit collects every emitted electron.
Frequency is measured in THz and absorbed photon flux is relative to the reference setting.

hypotheses.statement: Each absorbed photon ejects one electron only when photon energy exceeds a 2.00 eV work function; stopping potential is max(0, 0.0041357 times frequency in THz minus 2.00 V), independent of absorbed photon flux, and saturation current equals the relative absorbed photon flux in microamperes.

Emission begins only above 600 THz; above threshold stopping potential is 0.50 V times relative absorbed photon flux, while saturation current equals the relative absorbed photon flux in microamperes.
